title: Seneca: life is long enough
hook: Seneca argues we are not given a short life but make it short by wasting it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cato's last night, and the son and friends who tried to reach him. Reach out before morning stays true every night.

Where did the year go? I don't have time. Life is short. A Roman writer looked hard at that complaint and said no. Seneca: born in Spain, raised in Rome, Stoic philosopher, playwright, senator, and, awkwardly, an enormously rich man and adviser to the emperor Nero. A complicated man, who wrote a short essay still read today: On the Shortness of Life.
screen: `WHERE DID THE YEAR GO?` → `A ROMAN SAYS NO.` → `ON THE SHORTNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Most people, he says, even great thinkers, grumble that nature is stingy, that life runs out just as we're getting ready to live it. Then he turns it over. We aren't given a short time; we waste a great deal of it. Life is long enough, and generous enough, for the greatest things, if the whole of it is well spent. Poured out on distractions, on chasing what doesn't matter, on other people's errands we never chose, it's gone at the end before we ever noticed it passing. His picture is money. Hand a fortune to a careless owner and it's gone in no time; hand a modest sum to a careful one and it grows. Life works the same way. His Latin is short enough to remember: vita, si uti scias, longa est. Life, if you know how to use it, is long. Now the awkward part. Critics in his own time pointed out that a man this rich, this close to power, was lecturing everyone else about what matters. He knew it, and answered, in another essay, that he was describing the good life, not claiming he'd reached it. Honesty or excuse, the essay has outlived the argument. And notice what he isn't saying. Not cram more in, be more productive. The opposite: stop giving your life away to things you never chose, and you'll find more of it than you thought.
screen: `AN OLD COMPLAINT.` · `NOT SHORT, BUT WASTED.` · `A FORTUNE IN CARELESS HANDS.` · `A COMPLICATED GUIDE.` · then, large: `LONG ENOUGH, IF USED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Look back over today or yesterday and find one hour you gave away without really choosing to: scrolling, a meeting you didn't need, a worry on replay, a show you didn't even like. No guilt: imagine it back in your hands, and let one answer come for what you'd do with it.
Seneca. A rich, complicated Roman Stoic who argued that life isn't short, only wasted.
Your line: long enough, if used. Tomorrow, Seneca shows us how to keep the books. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many people who follow Stoic practice review their day each evening, as Seneca described doing, noticing where their time and attention actually went.

original.note: Latin, from Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2.1: life, if you know how to use it, is long.
